content: Human position refers to the specific configuration or arrangement of the human body. Various terms are used to describe human positions, each with distinct nuances: Position is a general term that describes the arrangement of the human body. Posture refers to a position that is either intentionally or habitually assumed. Pose implies a position taken with artistic or aesthetic intent. Attitude describes postures adopted for the purpose of imitation, whether intentional or not, and is also used in certain standard expressions to refer to specific types of postures. For example, Freud never assumed a fencer's attitude, yet almost all took him for a swordsman. Bearing refers to the manner in which a posture is held, including gestures and other aspects of conduct. Types of Human Positions When stationary, humans can adopt several primary positions, categorized by the type of support involved: Standing Although standing appears static, modern instrumentation reveals it involves subtle rocking movements from the ankle in the sagittal plane. This swaying motion is often compared to the movement of an inverted pendulum. Factors such as spring-like action in muscles, higher-level control from the nervous system, and engagement of core muscles contribute to maintaining balance. While standing itself is not inherently harmful, it can be associated with certain pathologies. Short-term issues include orthostatic hypotension, while long-term conditions may involve sore feet, stiff legs, and lower back pain. Sitting Sitting requires a horizontal support structure, such as a chair or the ground. Variations in sitting include positions with legs extended horizontally or seated on an inclined surface. When sitting on a chair, the shins are typically vertical, whereas sitting on the ground may involve crossed legs in the lotus position or legs folded horizontally under the thighs in a seiza position. Squatting Squatting is an intermediate posture between standing and sitting, where both feet remain flat on the ground, and the knees and hips are fully flexed, bringing the buttocks close to the heels. This position is often used for resting or working at ground level when the ground is unsuitable for sitting or kneeling. It is also the typical posture for defecation in regions where squat toilets are common. Additionally, squatting is a temporary position during lower-body exercises. Lying The lying position allows the body to assume a wide variety of shapes and orientations. The primary recognized lying positions include: Supine: Lying on the back with the face upward. Prone: Lying on the chest with the face downward (also referred to as lying down, laying down, or going prone). This is related to the term prostration. Side-lying: Lying on either side, with the body straight or bent forward or backward. Fetal position: A curled posture, with the limbs drawn close to the torso and the head near the knees. Kneeling Kneeling involves supporting the body on one or both knees or shins, which are approximately parallel to the ground. The feet may be positioned to raise the shins at an angle. The torso is typically upright but can vary depending on the specific kneeling posture. Hanging Humans can adopt various hanging positions, which occur when the support is located above the center of gravity. Hanging can be either voluntary or involuntary. Atypical Positions Atypical positions include standing on the arms, standing on the head, being on all fours, and other unconventional configurations.
